28.1 Introduction
Previous chapters examine the concepts, principles, and
design of operating systems for a computer that has a
single processor. This chapter considers how an operating
system can manage computation on a multicore processor.
The chapter starts with a brief description of multicore
hardware, and then considers how an operating system can
treat multiple cores as a unified resource when managing
processes.

28.2 The Move To Multicore Hardware
Recall that a circuit consumes power proportional to the
square of the clock rate. Because power consumption
generates heat, higher speed chips produce substantially
more heat. By the late 1990s, processor manufacturers
reached a situation where the density of transistors and
high clock rates reached the limit of the heat that could be
removed with air cooling, even with a fan attached directly
to the processor chip.
To solve the problem, the processor industry chose a
new direction: instead of trying to increase the clock speed,
use parallelism by placing multiple copies of a CPU on a
given chip. Industry uses the term core instead of CPU, and
multicore to characterize a chip that contains multiple
cores. In theory, two processors running at clock speed N
have as much processing power as a single processor
running at clock speed 2×N, but generate far less heat. The
processing power can be increased further by using four,
eight, or sixteen copies of the processor.

28.3 Multicore Hardware
To understand multicore operating systems, one must
understand the organization of the underlying hardware.
The details differ between vendors and models, especially
in cases where a chip contains more than four cores. Our
discussion will cover the basics by assuming a simplified

multicore design that includes the basic features common
to most multicore processors, and leave more advanced
designs for readers to explore. Figure 28.1 illustrates a
basic multicore processor and its external connections.

Figure 28.1 The architecture of a basic multicore processor
chip with an onboard bus connecting cores and a
connection to an external bus.

The figure shows three key components pertinent to
operating system design:
An onboard bus connecting all cores
An external bus connecting to shared
memory and I/O devices
A separate memory cache for each core
An onboard bus connecting all cores. Each multicore
chip includes a hardware mechanism that interconnects all
cores and provides a path to external components, such as
memory modules and I/O devices. Rather than adopt

terminology specific to any vendor, the figure uses the
generic term onboard bus to describe the interconnection
mechanism. In addition to allowing cores to communicate
directly with one another, the onboard bus allows an
arbitrary core to access memory and an arbitrary I/O
device.
More important, an operating system can configure the
hardware so that when a device posts an interrupt on the
external bus, the interrupt propagates to one of the cores
across the onboard bus.
An external bus connecting to shared memory and I/O
devices. Unlike a traditional symmetric multi-processor
system (SMP), multicore processors follow a shared
memory approach. That is, rather than each core having its
own physical memory, the physical memory for the system
attaches to the external bus, and all cores can access the
memory directly. Furthermore, all cores use the same
physical address for a given byte of memory.
A separate memory cache for each core. To make
memory access efficient, each core has its own L1 memory
cache. Some multicore designs arrange for groups of cores
to share an L2 memory cache. As the next sections explain,
the hardware for memory caching plays an especially
important role in multicore systems.

28.4 Multicore Cache Coherence Hardware

Because each core has its own memory cache, the
caches must coordinate to avoid inconsistencies. To see
why, consider how the sequence of events in Figure 28.2
leads to an inconsistency if the caches do not coordinate.

Figure 28.2 A sequence of events that leads to inconsistency
on a multicore processor that has uncoordinated
caches.

To avoid such inconsistencies, multicore designs include
extra hardware that coordinates the caches across all
cores. Known as a cache coherence system, the hardware
mechanism uses the onboard bus to inform other caches
whenever a core changes a cached value. As an example,
consider the steps in Figure 28.2 with a cache coherence
system in place. In step 4 when Core 1 updates variable X,
the cache coherence system informs other caches that their
cached value has become invalid † . Consequently, in step 5,
the cache on Core 2 will obtain the updated value from
memory.
The point is:
To achieve high performance, a multicore
design arranges for each core to have its own
memory cache. To guarantee consistency, a

multicore

design

must

include

a

cache

coherence mechanism that coordinates the
value for a given item across all caches.
† Invalidating the entry in other caches works better than updating the
value because it avoids keeping a value in a cache when a given core may not
reference the item again.

28.5 Mutual Exclusion On A Multicore System
Previous

chapters

explain

the

need

for

mutual

exclusion, and describe two mechanisms that an operating
system uses to achieve exclusive use of a resource. Chapter
6 describes disabling interrupts, and Chapter 7 describes
semaphores. As we have seen throughout the text, the
ability to disable interrupts forms a key building block of an
operating system for a single core processor because each
system call disables interrupts when it begins and restores
interrupts before returning.
Unfortunately, disabling interrupts does not guarantee
mutual exclusion on a multicore processor because each
core has its own interrupt mask. For example, if core 3
invokes the disable function, interrupts will only be
disabled on core 3, all other cores will continue to run with
their interrupt status unchanged. Thus, merely disabling
interrupts cannot guarantee mutual exclusion because
another core may continue to run simultaneously and may
change global variables.

To summarize:
Because disabling interrupts only changes the
status on one core, disabling interrupts on
one core does not guarantee mutual exclusion
because other cores that continue to run
simultaneously may change shared variables.

28.6 Mutual Exclusion With Hardware Locks
And Busy Waiting
How

can

an

operating

system

guarantee

mutual

exclusion on a multicore system? The answer lies in a
special hardware mechanism that multiple cores can use to
coordinate. Conceptually, we say that the hardware defines
a set of locks and provides instructions that a core can use
to lock and unlock any of the locks. The hardware
guarantees that if two or more cores attempt to lock one of
the locks simultaneously, one of them will succeed and the
others will fail.
Unlike the semaphore abstraction described in Chapter
7, the locking system used with a multicore processor does
not maintain a queue of cores waiting for a resource.
Instead, cores use an approach known as busy waiting. To
obtain access, a core must repeatedly execute the lock
instruction until the instruction returns a successful status.

Busy waiting makes no sense on a single-processor system,
but works well in a multicore situation.

28.7 Cache Coherence, Locks In Memory, And
Test-And-Set
Although early multiprocessor systems used separate
hardware for locks, modern multicore processors allow
programmers to use any location in memory as a lock.
Interestingly,

the

locking

hardware

relies

on

cache

coherence. Recall that when a core updates a memory
location, the cache coherence mechanism invalidates the
entry in all other caches. Furthermore, the cache hardware
coordinates across all cores and handles simultaneous
attempts to read and update a value.
To use a memory location as a lock, hardware usually
defines a zero to represent unlocked and nonzero to
represent locked. To unlock one of the lock locations, a
core stores zero into the location. Locking requires a
special instruction known as test-and-set. The test-and-set
instruction performs two operations atomically: it records
V, the current value of the location and then assigns a
nonzero value (e.g., 1). Finally, the test-and-set instruction
reports success if the initial value of V was zero and failure
if V was nonzero. If multiple cores simultaneously attempt
to test-and-set location L, the cache coherence hardware
guarantees the following:

If memory location L contains a nonzero
value before the attempt, the test-and-set
instructions in all cores will report failure.
If memory location L contains zero before
the attempt, the test-and-set instruction on
exactly one core will succeed, and will fail
on all other cores.
To summarize:
To implement mutual exclusion among cores,
multicore

systems

provide

a

test-and-set

instruction that atomically tests the value in a
memory location and changes the value. The
cache coherence hardware guarantees that if
multiple cores attempt to test-and-set the
same memory location simultaneously, only
one core will succeed.
Using memory locations as mutual exclusion locks
provides a significant advantage for an operating system
because the hardware does not limit the number of locks.
Thus, an operating system designer can choose the
granularity of locking (e.g., one lock for each module, one
for each system call, or one for each data structure). In a
system with many cores, fine granularity locking can
increase parallel execution substantially.

28.8 Multicore Operating System Design
Before multicore hardware appeared, industry followed
a

distributed

computers

computing

worked

approach

together

to

in

which

provide

a

multiple

computing

environment. In the distributed world, each computer ran
an independent operating system, and software on the
systems interacted by communicating over a computer
network or the Internet. Multicore systems differ in two
ways. First, the hardware provides a tight coupling among
cores on a chip, which means that communication among
cores
occurs
orders
of
magnitude
faster
than
communication over a computer network. Second, instead
of running an independent copy of an operating system on
each core, a single operating system runs that uses and
manages all cores on a chip. That is, the operating system
treats cores as a resource, and assigns computational tasks
to cores in a way that maximizes performance.
Operating system designers have experimented with
several approaches, including:
One core dedicated to OS functions
A subset of cores each dedicated to
one OS function
All cores run both applications and OS
functions
One

core

dedicated

management functions

to

power

One core dedicated to OS functions. Early multicore
systems arranged for one core (e.g., core 0) to run
operating system functions, and used other cores to run
applications. When an application process makes a system
call, the core running the application hands off the process
to the core that runs operating system functions. The
approach makes it easier to port a conventional operating
system to a multicore processor, but incurs a severe
performance penalty because the operating system core
can become a bottleneck.
A subset of cores each dedicated to one OS function.
Depending on the expected workload, dedicating one or
more cores to specific operating system functions may
improve performance. For example, consider demand
paging. Instead of waiting for a page fault to trigger page
replacement, the operating system can dedicate a core to
run

the

page

replacement

process

in

background,

continually scanning page tables, collecting unused pages,
and even writing dirty pages back to secondary storage.
Interestingly, some systems have the core that handles
page replacement compress existing pages and leave them
in memory, which avoids fetching a copy from secondary
storage if another reference occurs.
All cores run both applications and OS functions. The
operating system assigns an application to an arbitrary
core. When the application makes a system call, the core
running the application enters the kernel and executes the
appropriate system function. The approach means that the

cache retains values that the application has been using,
but has the disadvantage of requiring all system functions
to be rewritten to use test-and-set for mutual exclusion.
One core dedicated to power management functions.
Power management has become a key operating system
requirement for both portable and non-portable systems. A
multicore operating system can conserve power by shutting
down cores when they are not needed and starting
additional cores when they are needed. Using a separate
core to manage power makes sense because the decisions
require knowledge of the global state. For example, even if
one core becomes temporarily overloaded, the system
should not start an additional core unless other active cores
are also overloaded. Similarly, when a core becomes
underutilized, processes running on the core can be
migrated to other core(s) and the core can be shut down.
To make such decisions, power management software must
know the current load on all cores.

28.9 A Simplistic Scheduling Invariant For
Multiple Cores
How should an operating system schedule processes on
multiple cores? Recall that an operating system may
dedicate some cores to specialized tasks, and a power
management system may choose to shut down some cores
temporarily to conserve power. Therefore, the question

becomes, given a set of K available cores, how should an
operating system schedule processes to run on the cores?
A simplistic approach extends the scheduling invariant
used on a single-core processor. In particular, instead of
having exactly one process currently executing, the system
can have up to K currently executing processes, one on
each available core. Furthermore, to make scheduling
follow the process priority scheme in earlier chapters, the
scheduler invariant must specify that at any time, K highest
priority

processes

are

executing.

We

can

state

the

simplistic scheduling invariant as:
At any given time on a multicore processor
with K available cores, K highest priority
processes are executing. Among processes
with equal priority scheduling is round-robin.

28.10 Context Switching And Changing Cores
At

first

glance,

the

simplistic

scheduling

policy

described above seems reasonable. However, the multicore
hardware architecture prevents the policy from working
well. To understand why observe two facts. First, because
it chooses whichever core becomes free, that policy has
high probability of running each successive time slice of a
given process on a new core. Second, the presence of a
separate memory cache for each core makes switching

context to a new core relatively expensive. In addition to no
longer having cached values for a process's instructions
and data values, the new core will need to access page
table entries directly from memory. More important,
standard

optimizations

of

increasing

the

each

size

of

using

tagged

cache

do

values
not

and

improve

performance.
The point is:
A simplistic approach of scheduling the next
ready process on whichever core becomes
free does not perform well because it tends to
cause all cached values to be lost during the
context switch.

28.11 Multicore Scheduling Using Thread
Affinity
To avoid losing cached values on each context switch, a
multicore operating system can use an alternative
scheduling policy known as thread affinity. Thread affinity
scheduling binds each thread (i.e., each process) to a
specific core. The scheduling algorithm uses a per-core
approach: when a core becomes free, the scheduler selects
a ready thread from the core's affinity set. Because a given
thread will always run on the same core, a sufficiently large

tagged cache can preserve cached values, allowing a
thread to run again and again without penalty.
To summarize:
A

multicore

scheduling

policy

that

uses

thread affinity assigns a set of threads (i.e.,
processes) to each core, and arranges to
select from the affinity set when the core
becomes

free.

Doing

so

can

improve

performance because it retains values in the
cache.
Despite improving performance, thread affinity has
disadvantages.

First,

scheduling

code

becomes

more

complex. In addition to maintaining a ready list for each
core and selecting the next ready thread, the scheduler
must manage affinity sets. Suppose that after running for a
while, one core has a large set of processor-intensive
threads left in its affinity set and another core only has a
few I/O-intensive threads. The second core will run a null
process most of the time. The scheduler must monitor such
situations and adjust the affinity sets to balance the overall
load. Short-lived threads can mean that the load on a given
core can change quickly, making balancing difficult.
A second disadvantage arises from potential unfairness.
When it chooses a thread to run, the scheduler only
examines threads in a core's affinity set. As a result, a
scheduler that uses thread affinity may not enforce the

scheduling invariant globally. Consider, for example, a
situation in which the affinity set for core 1 contains six
threads with priorities 25, 24, 22, 21, 20, 20, and the
affinity set for core 2 contains four threads with priorities
23, 20, 20, 20. Affinity scheduling means core 1 will run a
thread with priority 25 and core 2 will run a thread with
priority 23. Because it has been assigned to the affinity set
for core 1, the thread with priority 24 will remain ready,
even though it has higher priority than the thread currently
running on core 2. We use the term priority inversion to
describe a situation in which a lower priority thread
executes while a higher priority thread remains ready but
not currently executing. A second type of unfairness can
arise if affinity sets have unequal size. For example,
suppose the affinity set for core 3 contains 20 threads of
priority 20 and the affinity set for core 4 contains 2 threads
of priority 20. Over a long period of time, the threads on
core 3 will each receive 1/20 of the processor's time, but
each thread on core 4 will receive 1/2 of processor time.
To avoid priority inversions and other unfairness, some
multicore schedulers assign equal priority to all application
processes and try to keep affinity sets approximately the
same size. If the sets do become unbalanced, the scheduler
can rebalance by reassigning one or more threads (with a
slight performance penalty when the threads context
switch to the new core).

28.12 Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT)

An additional hardware optimization increases the
performance on the most advanced multicore processors.
Known as Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT) † , the
optimization includes parallel hardware within each core
that can allow multiple threads to proceed in parallel
provided they do not need the same functional units. In
essence, the core has a small set of registers that each
contain state information for each thread, including an
instruction

pointer.

Before

execution

can

begin,

the

operating system stores appropriate values in the registers.
When the core runs, the SMT hardware looks at the
instruction that each of the threads is about to invoke. If
instructions do not need the same functional units in the
core, the SMT hardware allows them to execute in parallel.
If two or more of the threads need the same functional unit,
one of them proceeds and the others wait until the unit is
available.
An example will clarify how SMT works. Suppose the
operating system has configured three threads for SMT to
handle. Also suppose that at the current time, the next
instruction in thread A will perform a floating point
addition, the next instruction in thread B will perform a
right shift on an integer value, and the next instruction in
thread C will store a value into memory. Typically, floating
point arithmetic only uses the floating point register unit
and the floating point ALU, a right shift uses the integer
register unit and the integer ALU. SMT will allow the two
instructions to proceed in parallel. Depending on the

internal arrangement of functional units, thread C may also
proceed. However, if the value to be stored into memory
currently resides in an integer or floating point register,
and if a register unit can only be used by one instruction at
a time, the SMT hardware will block thread C until the unit
becomes available. In essence, the SMT hardware has
intimate knowledge of the internal structure of the core
and the units that each core uses.
To summarize:
Simultaneous
speeds

Multithreading

execution

by

allowing

hardware
multiple

threads to proceed simultaneously provided
the instructions they execute do not use the
same internal functional units.

28.13 Modifying Device Drivers For A Multicore
Processor
Recall that to avoid an I/O bottleneck, an operating
system must be designed to allow an arbitrary core to run
kernel code, which means an arbitrary core can invoke I/O
device drivers. As a consequence, a device driver cannot
rely on disabling interrupts to prevent interference, but
instead must implement mutual exclusion among cores. The
use of memory locations as locks means a designer can
choose a granularity: one lock for all I/O, one lock per

device, one lock for input on a device and one lock for
output, or other levels of granularity.
† Vendors also use proprietary terms, such as hyperthreading to describe
their versions of SMT.

Does an operating system designer need to make other
changes or invent new I/O policies to accommodate
multicore hardware? In most cases, output does not require
changes other than those for mutual exclusion. However,
input

and

interrupt

processing

do

require

changes.

Specifically, a designer must choose how to handle:
Cross-core notifications
Multicore interrupt processing

28.14 Cross-Core Notifications
Recall that when input arrives, a device generates an
interrupt, which causes the lower-half of the device driver
to run. On a single-core processor, the currently running
process continues to execute as the lower-half device driver
function runs. Further recall that some other process may
be waiting for the input, in which case the process
executing the lower-half will call a function that context
switches to the other process (e.g., the process running the
lower-half code signals a semaphore or sends a message).
A major difference occurs in a multicore design because
the process waiting for input may be running on a core

other than the core that handles the interrupt. The lowerhalf code can invoke mutual exclusion, make the process
ready (e.g., by signaling a semaphore), but cannot switch
context on the other core. Instead, a designer must arrange
a way for a process running the lower-half code on one core
to inform another core that its ready list has been updated
and it should call the scheduler.
What mechanism does an operating system use for
inter-core communication? The answer depends on the
hardware. Recall that the hardware includes an internal
bus that connects all cores. Some vendors provide an intercore message passing mechanism that allows a core to
send a message to another core or to all cores. Other
vendors provide a software interrupt mechanism that
allows a core to post a low-priority interrupt to another
core. Before receiving a software interrupt, a core must set
up dispatching and code that will handle the interrupt.
Because they share memory, cores can use the software
interrupt mechanism to pass messages — use mutual
exclusion to place the message in a core's queue and send a
software interrupt to the core. Arrange the software
interrupt handler on each core to use mutual exclusion to
extract the next message from the core's queue and then
process the message.
The point is:
Multicore hardware provides a mechanism
that a lower-half function can use to inform

another core that one of the processes
assigned to the core has become ready and
that the core needs to call its scheduler.

28.15 Multicore Interrupt Processing
When a device posts an interrupt on the external bus,
the multicore hardware passes the interrupt to the internal
bus. What happens next? Do all cores receive the interrupt?
Does one core (e.g., core 0) handle all interrupts? Modern
multicore hardware offers an operating system designer a
choice. The hardware allows an operating system to choose
which core handles a given device interrupt. We say that
the operating system chooses a core to handle each device,
and pins the interrupt for the device to the core. As an
alternative

terminology,

some

vendors

say

that

the

operating system specifies device affinity. Once the affinity
between a device and a core has been configured, the
hardware forwards the interrupt to the designated core
without interrupting other cores.
A typical policy attempts to balance the interrupt load
across multiple cores. Instead of pinning all interrupts to
one core, spread them across several cores. Furthermore,
balance the expected load based on the rate of interrupts.
For

example,

a

high-speed

network

interface

device

generates interrupts much more rapidly than a low-speed
device, such as a keyboard or mouse. Therefore, to balance

the load, a designer may choose to pin multiple low-speed
devices to one core, and only pin one high-speed device to
another core.
We can summarize:
Multicore

hardware

allows

an

operating

system to pin the interrupt from each device
to a specific core. Typically, instead of pinning
all interrupts to one core, an operating
system attempts to balance the interrupt load
by pinning interrupts to multiple cores.

28.16 Summary
Multicore systems offer a shared memory model where
each core has its own cache. To implement mutual
exclusion, cores use a busy waiting approach where
multiple cores can wait on a lock and the hardware
guarantees that only one will succeed in obtaining the lock
at a given time. Cache coherence hardware makes it
possible to use memory locations as locks, giving the
designer a choice in the granularity of locking.
Instead of using a scheduling policy that assigns the
next ready process to whichever core becomes free,
multicore schedulers use a thread affinity approach that
assigns each thread or process to a specific core. The
scheduler for the core selects among those threads that

have affinity to the core. Although it improves cache
performance, affinity scheduling may introduce global
priority inversions in which a thread with lower priority
runs on one core while a thread with higher priority
remains blocked because the core for which it has affinity
currently has an even higher priority thread running. To
avoid priority inversions, a multicore scheduler may choose
to make all application threads have the same priority.
Simultaneous

Multithreading

(SMT)

hardware

allows

multiple threads to run simultaneously on a core provided
they do not use the same internal functional units.
To allow arbitrary cores to access device drivers, the
drivers must be modified to have mutual exclusion among
cores (i.e., use locking and busy-waiting). An operating
system can pin each device interrupt to a specific core and
choose an interrupt affinity assignment to balance the
interrupt load across cores. A process waiting for input to
arrive may be assigned to a core other than the core that
handles the interrupt. Therefore, a lower-half may need to
use an inter-core message passing system or a software
interrupt mechanism to inform the core to which a process
has been assigned that one of its processes has become
ready and the core must therefore reschedule.

29.1 Introduction
Previous chapters examine the concepts and principles
that underlie the internal design of a basic operating
system. This chapter considers how operating systems
provide support for a variety of computing platforms,
including devices used in the Internet of Things, mobile
devices, devices used to provide network communication,
cloud computing facilities, and virtualized computation. It
discusses some of the special requirements that arise, and
describes ways the basic functionality covered in previous
chapters can be extended and adapted to handle the needs.

29.2 Embedded Systems

An embedded system consists of a control mechanism
placed “inside” a larger system. For example, a microwave
oven contains an embedded control system that receives
input from a keypad, starts and stops the tube that
generates microwaves, and controls the power level at
which the tube operates. Similarly an elevator contains an
embedded system that senses when buttons are pushed,
closes the door, moves the elevator to a selected floor, and
opens the door.
It may seem that an embedded control system could
consist of a single software program and an operating
system would not be needed. However, most embedded
systems cannot focus on one specific task at a time because
they must handle multiple events. For example, while the
embedded system in a microwave oven is counting down
the cook time, a user may open the door and the embedded
system must temporarily turn off power to the microwave
unit. Similarly, someone can press an elevator button for a
new floor while the elevator is already moving to a
previously-selected floor. An operating system that
supports concurrent processes and allows a process to wait
for a specific device makes it easier and safer to write
control code.

29.3 The Internet of Things (IoT)
Industry uses the term Internet of Things (IoT) to
describe a special case of embedded devices that use the

Internet to communicate. Many IoT devices are designed to
allow a human user to access the device remotely. For
example, a user can install an app on their smart phone
that allows them to control an IoT thermostat in their
residence. They can also install an app that allows a video
doorbell on their residence to contact their phone
whenever someone rings the doorbell.
It may seem that an IoT device dedicated to one specific
task, such as changing the temperature setting or sending
a video stream, would not require operating system
functionality. To support Internet communication, however,
the embedded system in an IoT device contains a protocol
stack. As we have seen, protocol software does not merely
run when an application sends a packet. Instead, Internet
protocols require a system to respond to packets that
arrive, even when no application on the device happens to
be using the Internet. Thus, even IoT devices that provide
trivial functionality need an operating system.
When they think of IoT devices, most people, think of
devices that consumers use. However, an additional set of
devices forms the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT).
Unlike consumer IoT devices, IIoT devices handle businesscritical tasks. For example, consider an automated factory.
Assembly lines in such a factory contain robots that each
perform a task as items pass down the assembly line. The
robots as well as the assembly line contain sensors that
continually monitor status, send reports to a factory control
system over a (wired or wireless) network, and accept

commands from the control system to slow or stop an
assembly line within a specified time after a problem has
been detected. To handle situations quickly, IIoT devices
need an operating system that allows a programmer to
assign a high priority to any process that must run quickly.

29.4 Mobile Systems
Although many workers use tablets and laptops daily,
the smart phone has become widely adopted as the
dominant mobile consumer device. Unlike other embedded
systems, mobile devices operate on battery power. As a
consequence, power conservation has become a major
design constraint, and having an operating system in a
mobile device can help conserve power. As the previous
chapter points out, running two cores at half speed takes
much less power than running one core at full speed;
running multiple cores at even slower speed can further
reduce power consumption. One optimization arranges for
a scheduler to spread processes evenly across multiple
cores. Hardware in mobile systems offers an operating
system two additional ways to conserve power while
allowing computation to proceed: sleep states and clock
rate adjustment.
Sleep states: Most battery-operated processors provide
a set of sleep states † that shut down parts of the processor,
causing it to consume less power. For example, an
operating system scheduler can monitor core use. When it

finds that the computational load has becomes light, the
scheduler can consolidate processes on fewer cores and
then place unused cores in a hardware sleep state.
Awakening the hardware from a sleep state requires extra
power as well as time, so before placing hardware in a
sleep state, the scheduler must compare the power that will
be saved during the sleep interval and the extra power
required

to

awaken

the

hardware.

To

accommodate

hardware sleep states, the operating system may need an
expanded set of process states.
Clock

adjustment:

The

hardware

in

some

mobile

systems permits the operating system to adjust the clock
rate. Because power consumption varies as the square of
the clock rate, reducing the rate can lower power
consumption dramatically. An operating system scheduler
can monitor the processes that are running, and then slow
down the clock to execute processes that do not need the
fastest processing time.

29.5 Unexpected Uses Of Operating Systems
Although it is small enough to fit into one's hand, a
smart phone contains a powerful processor, Gigabytes of
memory, and hundreds of Gigabytes of storage. A phone
can run many apps that use Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and the 5G
telephone network concurrently. In fact, the hardware in a
modern cell phone exceeds the hardware in a high-end
workstation of the 1990s. Consequently, everyone expects a

phone

to

run

a

sophisticated

operating

system.

Surprisingly, much smaller, less powerful devices also run
an operating system. We will consider two examples:
hearing aids and wearable devices.
Wearable devices. A small, wearable device can provide
continuous monitoring of the human body and medical
conditions. Athletes use wearable devices to monitor the
body under physical stress and respiration. Doctors use
both wearable and implanted devices to monitor and
control heart functions, blood sugar levels, and disease
symptoms.
Although it may seem that they do not need an
operating system, wearable devices can be quite
sophisticated. First, they perform local computation to
analyze readings, and the analysis usually involves looking
at trends across multiple measurements rather than merely
checking the level of each individual reading. Second, the
devices use network communication to upload readings for
the doctor to see. Normally, a device can conserve power
by only taking and uploading readings periodically (e.g.,
take a reading once a day and upload the readings once a
week). When the software encounters a situation where the
readings indicate danger, the device may choose to
perform readings more often, and upload them frequently.
An operating system can make it easier to assign each task
a high or low priority, and to change priorities dynamically
as conditions warrant.

†Note that hardware sleep states are unrelated to the sleep state used for
processes.

Hearing aids. Early electronic hearing aids consisted of
a device approximately two inches by four inches carried in
a shirt pocket. The device contained a microphone and
amplifier, with wires connecting small earphones that
protruded from a person's ears. By contrast, modern
hearing aids are marvels of technology. First, each device
is so small that it fits entirely into a human ear, with no
wires and almost no part visible. Second, each hearing aid
uses a digital signal processor tuned to amplify only the
frequencies that the individual cannot hear well. Third, the
hearing aids have a local network connection that allows an
audiologist to test an individual's hearing and adjust the
digital signal processor. Fourth, modern hearing aids have
a Wi-Fi receiver that allows theaters and other venues to
transmit audio directly to the hearing aids.
Although modern hearing aids seem incredibly tiny,
they run an operating system † . The OS allows them to
handle multiple network connections, run the applications
that allow an audiologist to test hearing and adjust the
frequencies to amplify, listen to concert audio, and allow
the user to adjust the volume.

29.6 Operating Systems In Network Equipment
Everyone who has an Internet connection knows that
their ISP requires them to have hardware devices that

attach their computers to the ISP's connection. An ISP
typically uses names such as modem, wireless router, or
Wi-Fi router. Companies often have an Ethernet switch
connecting desktop computers in offices to the corporate
network, and may give an employee a VPN router to use
when working at home. A large enterprise or an ISP may
have one or more Internet routers that handle higher speed
connections among networks.
Each of these hardware devices, including inexpensive
wireless routers used in a residence, run an operating
system; even switches that perform packet forwarding in
hardware run an operating system. An operating system
allows a network device to provide a way for a manager to
configure, test, and control the device. For example, a
wireless router may run a web server that allows a user to
change the wireless SSID and password, block certain
traffic, and control times when children can use the
Internet.

29.7 Operating Systems In The Edge/Fog/Cloud
Hierarchy
Most computer users have heard of cloud computing
and cloud services. Initially, cloud computing divided
computation into pieces: the user's local computer or cell
phone performed some computation, and all other
computation ran in the cloud. The cloud industry is moving
toward a hierarchy with tiny, edge data centers near each

user, several tiers of increasingly larger fog data centers
that each cover a larger geographic region, and large cloud
data centers at the top of the hierarchy.
The idea is to avoid network latency by performing
computation in the local device when possible, using the
edge when needed, and only moving up the fog hierarchy
when lower levels do not suffice. A cloud data center
handles

computation

when

none

of

the

edge

or

intermediate fog data centers suffices. Operating systems
at each level of the hierarchy can handle scheduling. They
can check for available resources before starting a
computation, monitor the load on equipment, and move a
computation up the hierarchy when necessary.
†At least one hearing aid company runs Xinu in their hearing aids.

29.8 Hypervisors, Virtual I/O Devices, And
Containers
Hypervisors. We use the term hypervisor for software
that allows multiple operating systems to run concurrently
on a single physical computer. Given what we have learned
about operating systems, it may seem impossible to have
them run concurrently. An operating system assumes that
it controls all memory, and has direct access to each I/O
device. Indeed, a hypervisor cannot run successfully on
hardware that only has two levels of privilege: user and
kernel. Instead, a hypervisor needs a third hardware

privilege level. Basically, the hypervisor “owns” the
physical computer, including all memory and all I/O
devices. The hypervisor runs at the highest privilege level.
It chooses a part of the physical memory for an operating
system to use, configures the hardware to allow the
operating system to access the chosen memory, and loads
the operating system into the memory. The hypervisor
arranges for all I/O operations to raise an exception. It then
starts the operating system running with kernel privilege.
When it executes non-privileged instructions, an operating
system uses the processor exactly as if it were the only
operating system on the computer. When the operating
system attempts to execute an instruction that requires
hypervisor privilege, the hardware raises an exception, and
control transfers to the hypervisor. We say that the
hypervisor provides a Virtual Machine for each operating
system.
Virtual I/O devices. As an example of privilege, consider
what happens when an operating system attempts to
access an I/O device directly. The hardware raises an
exception and traps to the hypervisor, which decides how
to respond. For a disk device, the hypervisor must have
allocated part of a physical disk to each operating system,
and only allows an operating system to access the part that
has been allocated to it. The key idea is that the hypervisor
hides the underlying hardware, allowing the operating
system to think that it has access to an entire disk. Of

course, the disk that the operating system sees is smaller
than the underlying hardware disk.
For other devices, the hypervisor responds to requests
in a way that allows an operating system to act as if it
controls

a

physical

device.

For

example,

when

the

operating system tries to access the network device, the
hypervisor responds exactly the same way a physical device
would respond. Instead of allowing the operating system to
control the network hardware, the hypervisor accepts
outgoing packets and sends them over the physical
network. The hypervisor also accepts incoming packets and
delivers them to the correct operating system. In each case,
the hypervisor responds to the operating system exactly the
way a network interface would respond, so the operating
system remains unaware that it did not control a physical
device. We say that the hypervisor provides a set of virtual
I/O devices.
Containers and efficient execution. Perhaps the most
remarkable aspect of the virtualization that hypervisors
provide arises from the efficiency. When an operating
system runs an application, the processor executes code at
full speed. Similarly, when an operating system runs, the
processor executes code at full speed. The processor traps
to the hypervisor when the operating system attempts to
access I/O devices or perform other privileged instructions
(e.g, shut down the computer).
When an individual user needs applications that only
run on another operating system, the user can run a

hypervisor,

and

boot

the

other

operating

system

temporarily. Cloud data centers make heavy use of
hypervisors

and

other

forms

of

virtualization.

A

virtualization technology, known as Docker containers, has
become particularly popular in data centers. Container
technology uses Linux Namespaces to allow each container
to run in a completely isolated environment. Unlike the
virtual machine environment that a hypervisor creates for
an operating system, a container works like a process — a
container can be created and run quickly, without starting
a new operating system. When code in the container needs
operating system services, the container passes requests to
the Linux system on which containers run.

29.9 Summary
A wide variety of devices and equipment runs an
operating system; the chapter provides a few examples.
Embedded operating systems control equipment ranging
from microwave ovens to elevators, and make control
software easier to write and safer. Although devices used in
the Internet of Things often perform straightforward
functions, most IoT devices run an operating system
because they include protocol software that needs to
respond to packets asynchronously.
As a special case of embedded systems, mobile devices
operate on battery power, and their design requires a focus
on power conservation. Operating systems in such devices

use hardware sleep states and adjust the clock rate to
reduce the amount of power used; reducing the clock rate
can

make

a

dramatic

reduction

because

the

power

consumed is proportional to the square of the clock rate.
Even tiny devices, such as medical monitoring systems and
hearing aids run operating systems.
Operating systems also run in each piece of network
equipment used to provide the Internet infrastructure, such
as

switches

and

routers.

Each

data

center

in

the

edge/fog/cloud hierarchy uses operating systems. Even
equipment used in residences, such as modems and
inexpensive wireless, run operating systems.
In addition to conventional operating systems,
hypervisors use operating system technology to permit
multiple operating systems to run concurrently on a given
computer. Cloud data centers use hypervisors and also
offer an alternative form of virtualization known as
Containers. Individuals can run a hypervisor on their laptop
to run applications that require an operating system other
than the operating system that usually runs.
